quests.instruction: Blindfolded, you are handed a lemon slice, and you know what it is before you taste it. Which two senses told you?
quests.hint: One is in your nose, and one is in your fingers.
quests.explanation: Your nose smells the sharp, fresh scent, and your fingers feel the cool, wet slice. Together, those clues tell you it is a lemon.
quests.funFact: The smell of a lemon comes mostly from oils in its peel.

quests.instruction: A beautiful song gives you goosebumps. Which chain of parts is working, in order?
quests.hint: The sound arrives first, and the goosebumps appear last.
quests.explanation: Your ears catch the music, your brain reacts to it, and the brain sends a signal that makes tiny muscles in your skin raise the hairs.
quests.funFact: About half of all people say they sometimes get chills from music.

quests.instruction: A sudden bright flash makes you squeeze your eyes shut. Which two parts act, in order?
quests.hint: One senses the light, and the other protects the eye.
quests.explanation: The retina senses the bright light and sends a warning, and then the eyelids close to protect the eye.
quests.funFact: Some people sneeze when they look at bright light, and scientists call this the photic sneeze reflex.

quests.instruction: A gymnast holds a handstand. Which two joints carry most of the weight and keep making small adjustments to stay balanced?
quests.hint: They are in the arms: one near the hands and one at the top.
quests.explanation: In a handstand, the arms hold you up, so the shoulders and wrists take the weight, and tiny adjustments in the wrists and fingers keep you from tipping.
quests.funFact: Gymnasts often practice handstand holds against a wall before they try them freely.

quests.instruction: You always write with your right hand. Today, you write with your left. Which half of your brain controls that left hand?
quests.hint: Think opposite: left hand, other side.
quests.explanation: The nerves cross over, so the right half of the brain mostly controls the left hand.
quests.funFact: Practicing with your other hand can help it become steadier over time.

quests.instruction: You hike up a steep hill on a hot day. Which three body systems work extra hard to keep you going?
quests.hint: One moves you, one delivers oxygen, and one brings oxygen in.
quests.explanation: Your muscular system powers each step, your circulatory system delivers oxygen to the muscles, and your respiratory system brings the oxygen in.
quests.funFact: Your heart rate climbs faster when you walk uphill than on flat ground.

quests.instruction: Clue 1: I am inside your chest. Clue 2: I come as a pair. Clue 3: I am soft and spongy, and I am not the heart. What am I?
quests.hint: You fill me with every breath.
quests.explanation: Lungs are the spongy pair in the chest. Kidneys are a pair, too, but they sit lower, toward the back.
quests.funFact: Lungs have no muscles of their own. The diaphragm and the rib muscles do the work of breathing.

quests.instruction: Clue 1: I am an artery. Clue 2: I am the biggest one in the body. Clue 3: I carry fresh, oxygen-rich blood from the heart to everywhere else. What am I?
quests.hint: I start at the left side of the heart.
quests.explanation: The aorta leaves the left side of the heart, arches over, and branches to carry blood everywhere.
quests.funFact: The aorta is about as wide as a garden hose.

quests.instruction: Clue 1: I am salty. Clue 2: I wash your eyes. Clue 3: I can run down into your nose and make it drip. What am I?
quests.hint: You make more of me when you peel an onion.
quests.explanation: Tears keep the eye clean and wet, and the extra drains away through the nose.
quests.funFact: Newborn babies usually start making real tears after a few weeks.

quests.instruction: You are about to ride a scooter. Which pair of gear protects your brain and the joints that catch you when you fall forward?
quests.hint: One covers the top of you, and the other covers the joints where hands meet arms.
quests.explanation: A helmet protects the brain, and wrist guards protect the wrists, which often take the first hit.
quests.funFact: Wearing a helmet greatly lowers the chance of a serious head injury.

quests.instruction: You touch a hot pan and get a small burn on your skin. After telling a grown-up, what should be done first?
quests.hint: Think of a gentle stream from a tap, not ice.
quests.explanation: Cool running water takes heat out of the skin and eases the pain, while butter and toothpaste can trap heat or cause infection.
quests.funFact: Doctors suggest running cool water over a small burn for about ten to twenty minutes.

quests.instruction: You twist your ankle at recess. Which plan helps most at first?
quests.correctAnswer: Rest, ice, wrap, and raise it 🧊
options: Rest, ice, wrap, and raise it 🧊
quests.hint: Think: slow down, cool it, support it, lift it.
quests.explanation: Rest keeps it from getting worse, ice and a gentle wrap limit swelling, and raising it helps fluid drain away. Tell a grown-up if it hurts a lot.
quests.funFact: Swelling is the body sending extra fluid to the injured spot, and it is a normal part of healing.

quests.instruction: Light is bent twice on its way to the retina. Which two parts bend it, in order?
quests.hint: One is the clear window at the front, and the other is the bendy focuser behind the pupil.
quests.explanation: The cornea bends the light first, and the lens then fine-tunes the focus so the picture lands sharply on the retina.
quests.funFact: The cornea does about two thirds of the eye's focusing.

quests.instruction: When you say "ahh," you can see a small bell-shaped bit hanging at the back of your mouth. What is it called?
quests.hint: It hangs down in the middle at the back.
quests.explanation: The uvula hangs from the soft roof of the mouth and helps keep food from going up into your nose when you swallow.
quests.funFact: The word uvula comes from a Latin word meaning little grape.

quests.instruction: Which small glands under your tongue and inside your cheeks make saliva?
quests.hint: They work harder when you smell food you like.
quests.explanation: Salivary glands release saliva into the mouth, and they work harder when you smell or see food you like.
quests.funFact: You have three main pairs of salivary glands.

quests.instruction: One part inside your ear is shaped like a snail shell, and another is stretched tight like a drum. Which pair is that, in that order?
quests.hint: The snail comes first, and the drum comes second.
quests.explanation: The cochlea is the coiled, snail-shaped part, and the eardrum is the thin skin that vibrates like a drum when sound arrives.
quests.funFact: An eardrum is only about nine millimeters wide, smaller than a coin.

quests.instruction: On a hot day, your forehead gets wet while you run. Which glands released that wetness to cool you?
quests.hint: They open onto your skin through pores.
quests.explanation: Sweat glands release sweat, and as it dries, it carries heat away from your skin.
quests.funFact: An adult has about two to four million sweat glands.

quests.instruction: Taste buds, smell sensors, and touch sensors in your skin all gather clues. Which of these needs air from your nose to do its job?
quests.hint: They live high inside your nose.
quests.explanation: Smell sensors catch scent particles carried in the air you sniff in, while taste buds work on your tongue and touch sensors work on your skin.
quests.funFact: The smell sensors in your nose are replaced every month or so.

quests.instruction: In the middle of your retina, a tiny pit gives you your sharpest vision. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is where your eyes aim when you look right at something.
quests.explanation: The fovea is packed with cone cells, so details look sharpest where you look directly.
quests.funFact: When you read, your eyes keep moving so that each word lands on the fovea.

quests.instruction: Which gland, tucked behind your breastbone, helps train germ-fighting cells and is largest in childhood?
quests.hint: It sits above your heart.
quests.explanation: The thymus trains white blood cells called T cells, so they can tell your own body from germs.
quests.funFact: The thymus is biggest in childhood and slowly shrinks after the teen years.

quests.instruction: With a stuffy nose, food tastes bland, but sweet and salty tastes still come through. Which part is still working?
quests.hint: It is on your tongue.
quests.explanation: Taste buds sense basic tastes, such as sweet and salty, even when your nose is blocked. The blocked part is smell, which adds most of the flavor.
quests.funFact: Mint feels cool because a chemical in it tricks the nerves that sense cold.

quests.instruction: On a high mountain, the air holds less oxygen. Which two parts speed up to make up for it?
quests.hint: One breathes faster, and the other pumps faster.
quests.explanation: Your lungs breathe faster to take in more air, and your heart beats faster to send oxygen to your muscles.
quests.funFact: After several weeks high up, the body makes extra red blood cells to carry more oxygen.

quests.instruction: Astronauts exercise for hours every day in space, because without gravity pulling on them, which two parts get weaker?
quests.hint: These are the parts that hold you up and move you.
quests.explanation: Bones and muscles stay strong by working against gravity. In space, there is little of it, so they weaken without exercise.
quests.funFact: Astronauts can grow a bit taller in space, because their spines stretch without gravity pressing down.

quests.instruction: Your body has an inner clock that tells you when to feel sleepy, and it is set mostly by light. Which part sends it the light information?
quests.hint: It is the part that sees whether it is day or night.
quests.explanation: Your eyes detect light and send the message to a clock in the brain, which helps set when you feel awake and sleepy.
quests.funFact: Some special light-sensing cells in the eye help set the body clock, even in people who cannot see.

quests.instruction: After a meal or a medicine, which two organs break down and clear out chemicals so they do not build up in your blood?
quests.hint: One breaks chemicals down, and the other sends them out as pee.
quests.explanation: The liver breaks chemicals down, and the kidneys remove what is left from your blood as pee.
quests.funFact: The liver turns a harmful chemical called ammonia into urea, which the kidneys then remove.

quests.instruction: You say a word out loud. Which two parts first make the sound and then shape it into the word?
quests.hint: One buzzes, and the other shapes.
quests.explanation: The voice box makes the sound, and the mouth, with the tongue and lips, shapes it into words.
quests.funFact: When you whisper, the vocal cords do not buzz, but your mouth still shapes the words.

quests.instruction: A tiny cluster of cells in the heart sends out the signal that starts every heartbeat. What is it often called?
quests.hint: It sets the rhythm.
quests.explanation: The natural pacemaker makes a small electrical signal that spreads through the heart muscle and makes it squeeze in order.
quests.funFact: If the natural pacemaker works poorly, doctors can fit a small artificial pacemaker.

quests.instruction: Right after you scrape your palm, which sequence of helpers goes into action, starting with the first one you notice?
quests.correctAnswer: Nerves, then platelets, then new skin cells ⚡
options: Nerves, then platelets, then new skin cells ⚡
New skin cells, then platelets, then nerves 🤚
quests.hint: You feel it first, it bleeds, and later it heals.
quests.explanation: Nerves send the pain message first, platelets plug the scrape, and new skin cells rebuild what was damaged.
quests.funFact: A scab is made of dried blood and a stringy protein called fibrin.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body cannot grow back if it chips, because it has no living cells?
quests.hint: It is the hardest material in your body.
quests.explanation: Enamel covers the outside of teeth and has no living cells, so it cannot regrow. Skin and bones are alive and can repair themselves.
quests.funFact: Fluoride can strengthen weak enamel, but it cannot replace enamel that is gone.

quests.instruction: Two senses are called the chemical senses because they detect tiny particles of substances. Which two are they?
quests.hint: One is in the nose, and the other is on the tongue.
quests.explanation: Smell and taste both detect chemicals, and together they create the flavors you enjoy.
quests.funFact: Butterflies taste with their feet.
